classification.difficultyReason: Divide units into sevenths and count steps to locate the fractions, carrying the same unit subdivision beyond 1.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is improper-mixed-numbers because the task represents a proper fraction and two improper fractions on a number line.
questions.methodNote: Use the equal-unit subdivision and counting method demonstrated in Example 1, replacing sixths with sevenths.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extend the demonstrated equal-subinterval method to sevenths and locate fractions beyond one.

classification.difficultyReason: Directly reproduce the taught sixths subdivision and count two, five and eight steps from zero.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill covers representing fractions with models; this task specifically uses a number line.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 divides each unit interval into six equal subintervals and counts markers from zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent three supplied fractions by equal subdivisions of a number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer each denominator from subdivisions within one unit, then express each marked position as a count of those fractional intervals.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied taxonomy has no dedicated fraction-number-line skill; representing fractions using models is the closest match.
questions.methodNote: Identify the denominator from the equal subdivisions of each unit and count those intervals from zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read fractions, including values above one, from three differently subdivided number lines.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest parts link improper fractions to whole squares and re-express the remainder using the supplied sixteenths or eighths, then produce another valid shading.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess area representations of fractions; d–f additionally require relating the denominator to the supplied finer partitions and using more than one whole.
questions.methodNote: A square has area 1. Divide it into equal-area regions and shade the required number. Example 2 on page 5 explicitly demonstrates different shading arrangements for one fraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent proper and improper fractions on supplied partitions and construct two different representations.

classification.difficultyReason: Count equal-area parts relative to one square and combine shaded parts across two squares while retaining the denominator for a single whole.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task identifies fractions directly from area models; equivalent forms record the source answers.
questions.methodNote: Count equal parts of one whole as the denominator and selected parts as the numerator; area examples permit different equal-area partitions and improper fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count equal shaded regions relative to one whole, including a total greater than one.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the selected quantity and total in familiar situations, including standard time and calendar units.

questions.mappingNote: Each part expresses one contextual quantity as a fraction of its total; g first expresses both times in minutes.
questions.methodNote: Use the total number of equal parts as the denominator and the number selected as the numerator, following the collection example on page 2.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the selected quantity and total in familiar situations, including standard time and calendar units.

classification.difficultyReason: Keep the explicitly defined whole fixed when comparing choices, distinguishing a quarter-square from one of four squares and eight sevenths from seven eighths.

questions.mappingNote: Both choices depend on retaining the given whole rather than redefining it as the total displayed collection or bar.
questions.methodNote: A fraction counts equal parts of the specified whole; page 5 demonstrates area models, and page 4 includes improper fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish the given whole from a collection or a longer bar when interpreting shaded fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the same whole-number multiplier for corresponding numerators and denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Question 3 directly assesses identification of that common multiplier, with a completed ×6 demonstration. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same original task.
questions.methodNote: Equivalent fractions are formed by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero whole number. Page 8 demonstrates multiplication by 3; pages 9–10 state the rule; Example 4 on page 11 applies whole-number multipliers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the same whole-number multiplier for corresponding numerators and denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Find unknown numerators or denominators by scaling equivalent fractions, simplifying first where necessary.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses equivalent fractions with an unknown component. Parts b and d combine simplification with multiplication; the other parts use one common scaling factor.
questions.methodNote: Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero whole number. Simplify by common factors before scaling when useful; Example 4 demonstrates finding missing fraction components.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find unknown numerators or denominators by scaling equivalent fractions, simplifying first where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each supplied division into equal spans across the dividend interval, coordinating unit subdivisions with jumps that cross whole-number boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts assess graphical interpretation of whole-number division as equal fractional lengths; the supplied mixed numerals are givens, not responses to calculate.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 illustrate division by splitting the complete interval from zero to the dividend into as many equal lengths as the divisor; each length is the quotient. Pages 3 and 5 establish equal fractional subdivisions of unit intervals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Illustrate supplied divisions by partitioning number-line intervals into equal lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the denominator to subdivide a unit and count the numerator's intervals beyond the given whole-number part.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 3 and 5 teach fractional number-line markers; pages 13–14 connect equal subdivisions and mixed numerals. The closest catalogue skill is improper-mixed-numbers because all four tasks represent mixed numerals.
questions.methodNote: Divide unit intervals into equal subintervals according to the denominator; locate a mixed numeral by moving the numerator's number of subintervals beyond its whole-number part.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Locate mixed numerals by dividing unit intervals into equal fractional steps.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert improper fractions to mixed positions, recognise equivalent halves, and place all three values on one consistently subdivided number line.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 3 and 5 demonstrate fraction placement on subdivided number lines. Pages 13–15 explain mixed numerals and conversion of improper fractions, supporting the locations of 22/4 and 68/8.
questions.methodNote: Partition unit intervals into equal subintervals; convert improper fractions to mixed numerals using whole-number division and simplify the fractional remainder.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert improper fractions to mixed numerals and locate three values on a number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert and simplify mixed fraction forms, then coordinate thirds and ninths on a shared scale, including a fraction that lands exactly on a whole number.

questions.mappingNote: Converting improper fractions and simplifying the fractional part of a mixed numeral identifies the whole-number intervals needed for the requested graphical representation.
questions.methodNote: Divide equal unit intervals into equal fractional subintervals, count markers and interpret improper fractions as whole numbers plus a proper fraction. Pages 3 and 5 demonstrate fractional number-line markers; pages 13–15 explain division and mixed-numeral conversion.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Locate six fractions and mixed numerals with different denominators on one number line.

classification.difficultyReason: Read fractional subdivisions beyond whole numbers and express the marked positions as mixed numerals.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess mixed numerals represented on number lines. Pages 3 and 5 establish equal subdivisions, page 9 supports simplification, and pages 13–15 connect fractional intervals and mixed numerals.
questions.methodNote: Count equal subintervals per unit to obtain the denominator, then count from the preceding integer. Write the position as a mixed numeral and simplify its fractional part.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read fractional subdivisions beyond whole numbers and express the marked positions as mixed numerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify a constant fractional increment and continue each sequence across whole-number boundaries.

questions.mappingNote: Each sequence directly assesses repeated addition of a fixed fraction. Mixed-numeral conversion supports crossing whole-number boundaries; no algebraic sequence formula is needed.
questions.methodNote: Continue by equal fractional steps; express totals crossing whole numbers as mixed numerals and simplify fractions. Pages 3 and 5 demonstrate equal fractional steps, page 9 establishes equivalence and simplification, and pages 13–15 explain improper fractions and mixed numerals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify a constant fractional increment and continue each sequence across whole-number boundaries.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret equal sharing as three divided by four and express each share relative to one bar; the supplied subdivisions support distributing quarters.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is to express three whole bars shared equally among four friends as the fraction 3/4; conversion between improper fractions and mixed numerals is not required.
questions.methodNote: Page 13 introduces equal sharing of whole objects and expresses three pizzas shared among five people as three fifths of a pizza. Page 14 states that dividing m by n gives m/n. Pages 3 and 5 establish equal parts of a whole.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent equal sharing of three whole bars among four people as a fraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct suitable fractions rather than compare supplied ones, choosing a useful denominator and checking proximity or both bounds of the requested interval.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks students to construct fractions satisfying approximate or interval comparisons; comparing fractions is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Use mixed numerals to interpret improper fractions and equivalent fractions with common denominators to compare values with benchmarks.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose examples of fractions near given benchmarks or between two familiar fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert improper fractions to mixed numerals and compare their fractional parts.

questions.mappingNote: Each part requires mixed-numeral conversion followed by comparison; comparison is the final assessed task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 14–15 convert improper fractions by division with remainder and simplify the fractional part. Pages 17–18 compare equivalent fractions with common denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Convert improper fractions to mixed numerals and compare their fractional parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Find equivalent fractions with a common denominator to identify the smaller fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly requests the common-denominator comparison method.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite fractions with a common denominator and compare numerators, as in Example 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find equivalent fractions with a common denominator to identify the smaller fraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend equivalent-fraction comparison to find exact midpoints, doubling denominators when needed.

questions.mappingNote: The task extends fraction comparison on a number line; comparison and equivalence are the closest supplied skills.
questions.methodNote: Extend the chapter's equal subdivision and equivalent-fraction methods: express endpoints with a common denominator that permits an integer midpoint numerator, then locate that numerator. The inspected teaching does not demonstrate a separate midpoint algorithm.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Extend equivalent-fraction comparison to find exact midpoints, doubling denominators when needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Justify a close comparison using equivalent fractions or distances from one.

questions.mappingNote: The worked answer applies the demonstrated common-denominator method; the concise answer also explains the teacher key's distance-from-one reason.
questions.methodNote: Example 9 compares close fractions by rewriting them with a common denominator and comparing numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Justify a close comparison using equivalent fractions or distances from one.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a shared tick interval and represent the addends as consecutive rightward jumps, interpreting endpoints that pass one whole.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts explicitly require number-line illustrations and use related denominators.
questions.methodNote: Represent addition by successive rightward jumps; use equivalent fractions to choose a common tick interval.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent additions with related denominators using successive number-line jumps.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose common denominators, add equivalent fractions, then simplify and convert improper sums to the requested mixed numerals; these are routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: Every part requires an improper sum expressed as a mixed numeral; parts j–l also require unrelated-denominator equivalence.
questions.methodNote: Find a common denominator using equivalent fractions, add, simplify and convert to a mixed numeral using division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add fractions with related or unrelated denominators and express simplified results as mixed numerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught common-denominator subtraction method and simplify, including recognising an improper result; no new strategy is needed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c use equal denominators; d–l require equivalent fractions before subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Example 12 subtracts numerators after expressing fractions with a lowest common denominator, then simplifies.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract fractions using common denominators and simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine three or four terms, including unlike denominators and a whole number.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the same common-denominator method to all terms, retaining each operation and the whole-number term in l.
questions.methodNote: Example 12d uses a common denominator for multiple terms; Examples 11 and 13 simplify and express improper results as mixed numerals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine three or four terms, including unlike denominators and a whole number.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct examples meeting an exact sum or an interval condition.

questions.mappingNote: Construct and verify sums using the taught addition method; a requires distinct fractions, while b and c do not.
questions.methodNote: Add fractions using a common denominator, simplify, and convert improper totals to mixed numerals.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct examples meeting an exact sum or an interval condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the complement of each fraction to one whole.

questions.mappingNote: Each missing addend is one minus the supplied fraction; simplify the result in b.
questions.methodNote: Represent a whole number as a fraction, then subtract using equal denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the complement of each fraction to one whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Add mixed numerals using common denominators and regroup improper fractional sums.

questions.mappingNote: All eight additions follow Example 13; b produces a whole-number result, while d, f and g require carrying an additional whole.
questions.methodNote: Example 13 adds whole numbers first, uses a lowest common denominator for fractional parts, and regroups an improper fractional total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add mixed numerals using common denominators and regroup improper fractional sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that both portions refer to the whole journey and add them using twelfths; the times only identify the two stages.

questions.mappingNote: Both portions refer to the complete journey; 'a further' signals addition, following Example 14a.
questions.methodNote: Add fractions of the same whole using the lowest common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret two successive portions of one journey and add fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the two separate colour categories as portions to combine, then add their fractions using a common denominator.

questions.mappingNote: The colour categories are separate portions of the same set of tiles, so their fractions are added.
questions.methodNote: Convert to equivalent fractions with a common denominator and add.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine two disjoint categories expressed as fractions with different denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the two age groups as separate portions of the same class and add one-third and one-fifth using fifteenths.

questions.mappingNote: Two mutually exclusive age groups belong to the same class, requiring the addition method of Example 14a.
questions.methodNote: Identify the required operation, form equivalent fractions, and add numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add fractions of two distinct age groups using a common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the remainder after a fraction of one litre is consumed.

questions.mappingNote: The word 'left' requires subtraction; the common-denominator rule applies to one whole litre.
questions.methodNote: Express the whole with the required denominator and subtract numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the remainder after a fraction of one litre is consumed.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer a missing addend and subtract using equivalent fractions.

questions.mappingNote: The section asks students to select the operation; a missing addend is found by subtracting the known addend from the sum.
questions.methodNote: Determine the required subtraction, convert to a common denominator, and subtract.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer a missing addend and subtract using equivalent fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a known difference to recover the smaller fraction.

questions.mappingNote: Example 14b establishes a difference context; here the known difference is subtracted from the larger fraction.
questions.methodNote: Select subtraction and use equivalent fractions with a common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a known difference to recover the smaller fraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that two equal fractions sharing a sum must each be half that sum.

questions.mappingNote: Equal sharing from page 13 and fraction equivalence/addition from pages 20–21 support finding the repeated addend without an untaught algebraic procedure.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions to express one third as two equal sixths, then verify by adding equal-denominator fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that two equal fractions sharing a sum must each be half that sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the nine unpainted-of-blue regions by subtracting seven from sixteen, then express the red count over the given total.

questions.mappingNote: The sixteen equal areas define sixteenths; the red remainder is the complement of seven sixteenths.
questions.methodNote: Subtract the known fraction from one whole using a common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the complement of seven of sixteen equal parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent slices as fractions, simplify, and combine portions of identical pies.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b establish the fractions; part c applies the addition method of Example 14a to identical wholes.
questions.methodNote: Express equal slices as fractions of a whole, simplify, and add using equivalent fractions with the lowest common denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent slices as fractions, simplify, and combine portions of identical pies.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret successive quarter totals, add fractions with different denominators and subtract the accumulated fraction from one whole.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess addition or subtraction of fractions. Part a combines two quarters, part b extends the total to three quarters, and part c finds the complement. Pages 23–24 establish the word-problem method and Exercise 4F identity.
questions.methodNote: Identify addition or subtraction from the word problem; form equivalent fractions with a lowest common denominator, combine numerators and simplify. For the remaining quarter, subtract the accumulated fraction from one whole. Page 21 subtraction examples supply the correct subtraction method despite the wording error in page 20’s summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret successive quarter totals, add fractions with different denominators and subtract the accumulated fraction from one whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Use improper fractions or taught regrouping to subtract across whole-number boundaries, then simplify and interpret the resulting proper fraction or mixed numeral.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses subtraction involving mixed numerals. Improper-fraction working is used for a–e, i, j and l; whole-number regrouping is used for g, h and k, and cancellation of equal whole-number components for f.
questions.methodNote: Examples 15 and 16 teach both regrouping one whole and converting mixed numerals to improper fractions, followed by common-denominator subtraction and simplification. Example 12 confirms subtraction of numerators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Subtract mixed numerals using common denominators, including regrouping and simplification.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret an unknown subtrahend and subtract mixed numerals with unrelated denominators, regrouping one whole.

questions.mappingNote: The unknown subtrahend equals the starting mixed numeral minus the remaining mixed numeral. Mixed-numeral subtraction is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions with a common denominator. Following Example 16 Method 1, regroup one whole before subtracting the whole and fractional components.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret an unknown subtrahend and subtract mixed numerals with unrelated denominators, regrouping one whole.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover the larger number by adding the given difference to the smaller mixed numeral, using a common denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Although located in Exercise 4G, this independent word problem directly assesses addition of mixed numerals with unrelated denominators. The lowest common denominator of 21 and 28 is 84.
questions.methodNote: Use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to recover the larger number. Follow Example 13 on PDF page 22: combine whole numbers, express fractional parts with their lowest common denominator, then add and simplify.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover the larger number by adding the given difference to the smaller mixed numeral, using a common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify subtraction as the inverse operation and subtract mixed numerals using a common denominator.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 gives a sum and one addend, so recover the other addend by mixed-numeral subtraction. No regrouping is necessary.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions with a common denominator, subtract the whole and fractional components, and simplify, following Example 15 Method 1 and Example 16 Method 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify subtraction as the inverse operation and subtract mixed numerals using a common denominator.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert mixed and whole numbers to a common fractional representation, preserve each addition or subtraction sign, and simplify the combined result.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess addition and subtraction of mixed numerals. Part a combines addition and subtraction; part b subtracts two mixed numerals successively. The supplied reuse candidates have different complete tasks and cannot be reused.
questions.methodNote: Examples 15 and 16, Method 2: convert mixed numerals to improper fractions, express them with a common denominator, calculate, simplify and convert to a mixed numeral. Examples 11–13 support common-denominator arithmetic and mixed-numeral addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine several mixed numerals using common denominators and simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret a verbal combination of a sum and a difference, then calculate with mixed numerals and common denominators.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 requires evaluating a sum and a difference of mixed numerals, then subtracting the latter from the former; add-subtract-fractions directly covers all assessed calculations.
questions.methodNote: Use equivalent fractions with a common denominator. Example 13 adds whole and fractional components; Examples 15 and 16 permit conversion to improper fractions for mixed-numeral subtraction. Simplify the final result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret a verbal combination of a sum and a difference, then calculate with mixed numerals and common denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct both taught representations by choosing equal partitions from the denominator and using the numerator to locate a point or shade regions.

questions.mappingNote: Page 3 introduces equal number-line intervals; page 5 Examples 1 and 2 demonstrate the two requested representations. The selected skill is the closest available match for representing fractions with area models.
questions.methodNote: Partition each unit interval into denominator-many equal subintervals and count numerator-many steps from zero. Partition a square or rectangle into denominator-many equal-area regions and shade numerator-many regions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Represent two proper fractions using equal intervals and equal-area parts.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the selected quantity and the corresponding whole in familiar situations.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 explains numerator and denominator using three occupied cups out of four; page 3 applies the same method to three spotted frogs out of five. Each situation here requires identifying the selected quantity and its whole, with weeks converted to days in part a.
questions.methodNote: Write the number of selected parts as the numerator and the total number of equal parts in the whole as the denominator.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the selected quantity and the corresponding whole in familiar situations.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the greatest common factor of two given whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess identifying the HCF of two whole numbers, matching hcf-two-numbers. No prime-factorisation algorithm or earlier-chapter teaching is assumed.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 explicitly considers all factors of the two numbers to identify their highest common factor. Page 11 Example 5 uses the HCF when simplifying a fraction. Worked answers list factors and select the greatest shared value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the greatest common factor of two given whole numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the lowest common multiple of three pairs of positive integers by listing multiples.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess finding an LCM. Worked answers use listing multiples, consistent with the inspected instruction, without introducing prime factorisation.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 explicitly instructs students to examine multiples until finding the lowest common multiple. Page 21 uses LCMs to obtain common denominators.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the lowest common multiple of three pairs of positive integers by listing multiples.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify common factors to simplify each fraction and use quotient and remainder to express improper fractions as mixed numerals.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 explains simplification by common factors and page 11 Example 5 applies the HCF. Pages 14 and 15 explain mixed numerals and conversion by division. Parts a and f require simplification only; parts b–e also require mixed-numeral conversion.
questions.methodNote: Divide numerator and denominator by their highest common factor. For an improper fraction, separate the whole-number quotient and the remaining proper fraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Simplify numerical fractions using common factors and convert improper fractions to mixed numerals.

classification.difficultyReason: Select common denominators for the additions, then simplify and convert improper results to mixed numerals using the taught sequence.

questions.mappingNote: Page 20 explains common-denominator addition; page 21 Example 11 demonstrates related and unrelated denominators, simplification and mixed-number results. These methods apply directly to all eight parts.
